all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: immersive experience
concepts.definition: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

defining_facts.text: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

concepts.name: virtual tour
concepts.definition: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

defining_facts.text: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

The digital heritage preservation system for Majuli island has two components: preservation, which produces the content of the virtual tour, and experiencing the heritage through immersive virtual tours, which allow users to explore the island virtually.

Majuli island's distinct tribal cultures are present in tribal villages that dot the landscape, its three major tribes are Mishing, Deori, and Sonowal Kacharis, each of which is supposed to have a distinct tangible and intangible cultural identity, and the villages' unique traditions and customs should be reproduced in a virtual tour.

concepts.name: user interaction
concepts.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

defining_facts.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

concepts.name: presence
concepts.definition: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

defining_facts.text: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer.

Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.

The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

The goal of any virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning that people believe they are in the real world while they are actually in a virtual world, and the closer a VR system is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides.

Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience.

Mark Weiser's quote that the most profound technologies are those that disappear and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment.

The key concerns to be addressed in the Majuli Island virtual reality (VR) Tour are capturing both the tangible and intangible aspects of the island's cultural heritage, which is the broader objective, the user experience, specifically the extent to which users feel present in the virtual island, and minimizing the risk of cyber sickness while users explore the island.
Presence is a psychological state of mind that is measured by standard questionnaires.
The QEP questionnaire was used to measure presence, and it is a 2004 revised version of the standard presence questionnaire (PQ).

The presence measure used to evaluate the virtual tour of Majuli Island included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, and visual fidelity, and tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity was additionally reported for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island.

The overall user presence ratings for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were involvement mean 5.65 (standard deviation 1.11, coefficient of variation 0.19), interface quality mean 4.37 (standard deviation 1.4, coefficient of variation 0.32), adaptation and immersion mean 5.4 (standard deviation 1.13, coefficient of variation 0.2), and visual fidelity mean 5.79 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.16).

The presence ratings for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island were tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity mean 5.68 (standard deviation 1, coefficient of variation 0.177), involvement mean 5.83 (standard deviation 1.05, coefficient of variation 0.18), interface quality mean 4.72 (standard deviation 1.36, coefficient of variation 0.33), adaptation or immersion mean 5.61 (standard deviation 1.15, coefficient of variation 0.22), and visual fidelity mean 5.94 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.15).

The overall presence results for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were summarized as good presence, meaning that users felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while virtually exploring Majuli Island.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.
Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

concepts.name: teleportation
concepts.definition: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

defining_facts.text: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement.

Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.

Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required.

concepts.name: locomotion technique
concepts.definition: Locomotion techniques, alternatively travel techniques, are techniques employed to let a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and to perceive that travel has taken place.

defining_facts.text: Locomotion techniques, alternatively travel techniques, are techniques employed to let a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and to perceive that travel has taken place.

Travel in navigation can be accomplished using four broad types of locomotion techniques: walking-based locomotion, steering-based locomotion, selection-based locomotion, and manipulation-based locomotion.

In the four broad locomotion technique types, object manipulation may not be involved in walking-based, steering-based, or selection-based locomotion; manipulation-based locomotion involves navigating by manipulating certain things, and navigation mostly involves no object manipulation while manipulation is not entirely avoided when implementing travel techniques in an immersive setting.

concepts.name: interaction design
concepts.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

defining_facts.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

concepts.name: user feedback
concepts.definition: In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

defining_facts.text: In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

concepts.name: code design
concepts.definition: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.

defining_facts.text: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, code design is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.

concepts.name: contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.

defining_facts.text: Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.

Contextual inquiry is a method more than 30 years old, whose importance in user-centered design was highlighted in 1988 under the term phenomenological research method, and by the end of the 1990s it had become well developed and popular.
Contextual inquiry is often referred to as a semi-structured interview process that consists of both interviews and observations.

The primary objective of contextual inquiry is to watch and observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting, that is, their work context, in order to gather more insight about user behavior and end-user requirements.
The interview part in contextual inquiry may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify certain behaviors or activities.
A well-planned contextual inquiry process generally takes one to two hours.

Observations and interaction with users in contextual inquiry enable designers to learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints at the workplace, which supports design decisions.

Contextual inquiry is important in system development because it studies users, such as managerial staff, in their work setting, reveals their unique behavioral traits, and enables design refinement; without it, designers may create invalid designs and give essential user activities equal importance to unnecessary features, compromising usability.

User activities observed in contextual inquiry must be supported as features in the system design; in the calendar app for managerial staff, the observed activities are setting meeting dates and reminders, so the app must support them to be usable for that user group.
Contextual inquiry is a usability requirement-gathering method that observes targeted or specified groups of users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave and what they do.

Contextual inquiry can be performed in two broad modes: active mode, where the observer is physically present in the environment where the users are doing their tasks, and passive mode, where no observer is present, user activities are recorded or videotaped and later observed by the observer, and issues are clarified through interaction with the users.

In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, the master-apprentice model, learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave; such advice is prohibited.
The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.

The plan stage of contextual inquiry involves identifying the goals of observation, gathering knowledge about the task domain, planning arrangements for recording observations, identifying the users and the date, time, and place of the observation, and, as a helpful practice, scripting and rehearsing the procedure.

The initiate stage of contextual inquiry involves obtaining all necessary permissions from relevant authorities before observing employees in their workplace and opening communication with end users to remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them, so that they behave naturally.
The execute stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the actual inquiry takes place, through performing observations and recording data.

The close stage of contextual inquiry ideally involves formally closing by sending thank-you notes or a message of gratitude to the users and possibly the authorities, because such users may be useful for future activities such as usability testing.
The reflect stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the observer or experimental team analyzes the data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals.

The affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to arrange the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals.
The outcome of contextual inquiry, a usability requirement gathering method, can be utilized as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles, and also as functional requirements.

Contextual inquiry (CI) in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was conducted after the user groups were identified, on samples from those user groups, to learn their needs and expectations, identify the system features to be supported for each group, and identify specific issues for those groups related to broad design challenges.

The large geographical area and cyber sickness challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was addressed by allowing each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, with each subset identified through contextual inquiry (CI) based on what that group typically does.

Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design.
Contextual inquiry is one of many methods available for usability requirement gathering.

concepts.name: interface design
concepts.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

concepts.name: interactive system development lifecycle
concepts.definition: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

defining_facts.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

The book Human-Computer Interaction, User-Centric Computing for Design discusses the stages of interactive system development life cycles in more detail with respect to broader interactive system development concerns.

The final design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was developed using the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDL) model, an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle that started with a design based on design guidelines and continuously refined design ideas from feedback and observations obtained by involving end users passively or actively.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.
The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality (XR) systems.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

concepts.name: tangible heritage
concepts.definition: Tangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts like masks and musical instruments and the architectural aspects of Satras and traditional tribal homes.

defining_facts.text: Tangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts like masks and musical instruments and the architectural aspects of Satras and traditional tribal homes.
Before Majuli disappears, it is essential to preserve its tangible heritage, intangible heritage, and ecological heritage.

concepts.name: intangible heritage
concepts.definition: Intangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed, including traditional skills, knowledge, and aesthetic norms in music, dance forms, drama or performing arts, mask making, vernacular architecture, weaving, food, and agricultural practices, and it is typically embedded in the daily and occasional activities of social life.

defining_facts.text: Intangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed, including traditional skills, knowledge, and aesthetic norms in music, dance forms, drama or performing arts, mask making, vernacular architecture, weaving, food, and agricultural practices, and it is typically embedded in the daily and occasional activities of social life.
Before Majuli disappears, it is essential to preserve its tangible heritage, intangible heritage, and ecological heritage.

concepts.name: location awareness
concepts.definition: Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design.

defining_facts.text: Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design.

concepts.name: navigation
concepts.definition: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

defining_facts.text: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.
The goal of navigation in a virtual world is to move the user from one point to another, which means a change of the user's field of view or viewpoint.
The movement involved in navigation in a virtual world has two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.
Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

concepts.name: ray casting
concepts.definition: Ray casting is the most basic way to extend a ray in pointing-based selection, in which the user points at objects with a virtual ray.

defining_facts.text: Ray casting is the most basic way to extend a ray in pointing-based selection, in which the user points at objects with a virtual ray.

In ray casting, selecting small distant objects is difficult and can require practice because the ray must be pointed precisely, and the difficulty increases when the small object is surrounded by other objects of similar, smaller, or larger size.

Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely, and a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending.

Depth ray is an improvement over basic ray casting in which a user-controlled depth marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, disambiguates multiple intersected objects and selects the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER) is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique that mixes ray casting, a pointing-based selection method, with hand manipulation, so selection and manipulation are integrated and the user does not need to perform them separately.

In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), the user selects an object using a ray casting technique, and when the ray intersects the desired object, the user's virtual hand moves automatically to the object and attaches to it, rather than the ray being attached to the object.

concepts.name: wayfinding
concepts.definition: Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

defining_facts.text: Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.
Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

Wayfinding is essentially a mental model, and the goal of wayfinding is to build a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment so that it is easier to locate oneself and identify a suitable path.

For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively.
Landmark support for wayfinding uses obvious distinct non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

Map support for wayfinding can provide maps of the space or place, such as a copy of the virtual world map, where the term world means the virtual world rather than the real world, or a world in miniature display that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points.
Path following support for wayfinding can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.

Breadcrumb support for wayfinding leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.
A compass or another direction indicator can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space, and a compass can be designed and placed in the environment.

never_defined.name: virtual world
never_defined.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

never_defined.name: realism
never_defined.definition: When creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the uncanny valley effect means that trying to match reality exactly with human-like figures or realistic objects may not produce a good experience if their human-likeness falls in the uncanny valley, so there is a trade-off over how much realism to include.

never_defined.name: 360-degree video
never_defined.definition: The highest representational fidelity is indicated by very good photorealistic immersive film content, such as 360-degree video or images of the real world in a virtual environment, while extremely low representational fidelity is indicated by purely abstract and non-objective worlds that are unfamiliar in real-world experience.

never_defined.name: orientation
never_defined.definition: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

never_defined.name: user experience
never_defined.definition: Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

never_defined.name: anxiety
never_defined.definition: Emotional conditions at the time of use can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness: negative emotions such as anxiety, stress, and frustration are typically associated with it, and personality traits such as neuroticism may also increase the likelihood.

never_defined.name: joystick
never_defined.definition: In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

never_defined.name: button
never_defined.definition: Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional model
never_defined.definition: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

never_defined.name: illumination
never_defined.definition: Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate.

never_defined.name: system design
never_defined.definition: Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.

never_defined.name: direction
never_defined.definition: The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

never_defined.name: Majuli virtual reality tour
never_defined.definition: Usability requirements for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour were gathered by making field trips to Majuli, interviewing people, observing people in their natural work settings, and collecting data in the form of notes.

never_defined.name: destination
never_defined.definition: Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

never_defined.name: user experience design
never_defined.definition: The design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was framed by its broader objectives of capturing tangible and intangible heritage, enhancing user presence, and minimizing cyber sickness, with corresponding design considerations of user experience design, exploration of the island, and handling cyber sickness.

never_defined.name: notification system
never_defined.definition: User feedback and interaction with users for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour led to incorporated design elements such as a minimap, a notification system, and user controls.

never_defined.name: icon
never_defined.definition: Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

never_defined.name: quality of experience
never_defined.definition: Preprocessing of the collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and the user's quality of experience involved using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements, such as the tripod of a 360-degree camera or its shadow.

never_defined.definition: The images and videos, mostly the images, were edited with image editing tools for uniform illumination because the 360-degree images captured at different times have different illumination and changing illumination while the user moves from one image to another will make the user feel that something is odd.

never_defined.name: ambient sound
never_defined.definition: Ambient sounds such as temple bells, birds chirping, and bike horns were added and played depending on the place being visited to enhance realism and create an authentic ambience, with temple bells played for a satra or a religious site.

never_defined.name: volume controller

never_defined.name: local orientation
never_defined.definition: A minimap is a world-in-miniature map for a specific place on the island, such as a village or town; it differs in appearance from the global island map and is provided at each of the island's 24 information points to give the user a sense of belonging or local orientation to that place.

never_defined.name: cultural video
never_defined.definition: At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface.

never_defined.name: local interface
never_defined.definition: For location awareness, the system uses dual maps: a global map, which is a world-in-miniature map of the entire island, on the tablet interface and a local minimap on the local interface, to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.

never_defined.name: orientation awareness
never_defined.definition: The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind.

never_defined.name: island tour
never_defined.definition: In the island tour, each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another.

never_defined.name: navigation arrow
never_defined.definition: Navigation arrows guide the user from one image to another, prevent random movement, and create a seamless exploration experience while supporting smooth travel.

never_defined.name: walking-based navigation
never_defined.definition: Walking-based navigation is used for a single spot, but exploring the entire island by walking-based navigation would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness, so a different travel technique was required.

never_defined.name: seated viewpoint
never_defined.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle when it is selected, changes the surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion, and lets the user operate the vehicle through ray casting interactions to provide a direction of movement and select a destination, to which the vehicle moves.

never_defined.name: selection-based locomotion technique
never_defined.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

never_defined.definition: The virtual tour system's tablet interface shows a list of videos available for a given spot, and when the user is at a spot the corresponding material for that spot is added to the interface so the user can choose it, giving access to the most relevant information for that spot, and that relevant information is also determined by the user type.

never_defined.name: point-of-interest awareness
never_defined.definition: In the virtual tour system, point-of-interest awareness is supported by directional arrows that indicate which way to move and guide users toward points of interest, and by information icons that, when selected, provide further details about the place, mostly as textual information, so users do not overlook important elements in the environment.
